title: Your own dharma
hookLine: your own path, done badly, beats someone else's done well
carry: svadharma: your own dharma, even imperfect
last: THE THREE GUNAS — NOTICE THE THREAD.

cards: Remember what Arjuna said in chapter two, slumped in the chariot? Better to live by begging, like a holy man, than to kill his own teachers.
He was reaching for someone else's life, one that looked purer than the life in front of him.

Krishna answered in chapter three with a line he now repeats in chapter eighteen, almost word for word: your own dharma, even done imperfectly, is better than someone else's, done well. But the verses around it need care.

teach.h: FOUR VARNAS, BY QUALITY AND WORK.
teach.b: Verses forty-one to forty-four describe the four varnas, the classes of ancient Indian society: brahmins, kshatriyas, vaishyas and shudras. Their work, Krishna says, is divided by the qualities born of their nature.
Calm, self-control, learning and faith for brahmins. Courage, skill and generosity for kshatriyas, Arjuna's class of warriors. Farming, cattle and trade for vaishyas.
Service for shudras. This is where honesty matters. You met a classmate's version of this question on day ninety-five; here it is in the Gita itself.

teach.h: USED TO DEFEND CASTE BY BIRTH.
teach.b: These verses have been used to support caste as a hierarchy fixed by birth, and people were deeply hurt by it. The reformer B. R.

Ambedkar criticized the Gita sharply for this. Some modern Hindu teachers read varna as temperament and calling rather than birth, pointing to chapter four, where Krishna says the four were made by quality and action.
Hindus still disagree about this, and the disagreement is real. Then verse forty-five turns to the heart of the passage: a person who is devoted to their own work reaches perfection.
Verse forty-six: by worshiping, through their own work, the one from whom all beings come, a person reaches perfection.

In this verse, work itself becomes worship. Verse forty-seven: better your own dharma, even imperfect, than another's, even done well. Verse forty-eight adds: don't abandon the work that's yours, even if it has flaws.
Every undertaking is wrapped in some fault, the way fire is wrapped in smoke.
Whatever one makes of the varna verses, these last four teach svadharma: each life has its own right work, and doing it, smoke and all, can be worship.

how: Some Hindus understand svadharma as the duties that belong to their own life and stage of life, and offer their daily work as worship; how the Gita's varna verses relate to birth-based caste is still debated among Hindus.

games.q: you're a warrior like Arjuna, and a quieter, more scholarly life looks better. what does verse 47 say?

practice: Think of a life you've envied lately, let it come fully into view, then gently set it down. Now think of the work actually in front of you, your family, your work, your studies, and notice its imperfections, the smoke.
Then notice the fire, the part that's truly yours, that no one else could do quite the same way.
If you pray, offer the next hour of it to God, as verse forty-six describes; if you don't, give it your full attention, and rest there.

wordCard.voice: Svadharma, one's own dharma. Gita eighteen: your own dharma, even imperfect, is better than another's done well; your own work can be worship.

orig.note: Sanskrit: svadharma, one's own (sva) dharma: the duty and path that belong to you; Gita 3.35 and 18.47.

carryVoice: Your line: svadharma, your own dharma, even imperfect. Your work can be worship. That's day two hundred twenty-two.
